payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is a recognizable frog visible in the toilet bowl opening or directly at its rim?
node.criteria: Pass if a recognizable frog is visible within the bowl opening or directly at its rim. Fail if that region is assessable and contains no recognizable frog. Unknown if frog identity or visibility of that region is insufficient. Identify the candidate and its visible location; this check does not establish that the frog is inside the bowl or that the request is complete.
node.binding: Inspect the edited image using the source toilet as the reference. Distinguish the bowl opening and rim from the raised lid, tank, surrounding fixtures, and floor. Frogs exclusively on those other surfaces do not pass this check.

node_traces.evidence: A recognizable green frog is visible inside the toilet bowl opening, resting on the inner bowl. Other frogs appear on the raised lid, tank area, and floor, but the bowl frog satisfies this check.

fulfillment: The node’s binding asks whether a frog is inside the bowl, but its completion criterion treats any visible frog within the rim as completed placement. In the edited image, the frog is perched across the bowl opening/rim rather than clearly placed down inside the bowl cavity; the other frogs are on the lid/tank area and floor. This supports visible progress, not necessarily full fulfillment. Tighten the semantic distinction between a frog merely overlapping or straddling the opening and one actually placed inside the bowl, and ensure the final decision applies that distinction to the same candidate across s1–s3. Do not count repeated dependent observations as independent corroboration. The traces are valid and queried with no transport or schema failures; the mismatch is semantic/criterion calibration, not missing evidence. Treat the reference label as an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth, and avoid forcing partial when the visual evidence genuinely establishes completed placement.
s3: The binding is underspecified: “opening or resting on an exterior toilet surface” can blur the key distinction between a frog merely overlapping/straddling the rim and one actually occupying the bowl interior. Make the node assess the same identified candidate’s body position against the inner rim and visible cavity, explicitly separating rim/lid/tank/floor placements from interior placement; do not let 2-D overlap alone establish completion. Preserve the existing pass/fail/unknown distinctions, including uncertainty when compositing or occlusion prevents a reliable judgment. The edited image shows frogs on the lid and floor and one in the bowl opening; evaluate whether that bowl frog is genuinely seated within the cavity rather than assuming either outcome from the aggregate label. Repeated high-confidence traces are dependent observations, not independent corroboration. This is a semantic criterion/binding issue, not a transport or schema failure; use the partial reference only as an aggregate constraint, not atomic ground truth.
s2: The binding should make the node distinguish progress from completion, rather than treating any frog visible within the bowl opening as proof of completed placement. In this edit, compare the same candidate against the source and assess its body relative to the inner rim and visible cavity: the frog appears to straddle the opening, which is progress, while frogs on the lid/tank and floor are unrelated to the requested placement. Keep the criterion evidence-based—do not infer completion or partial solely from the aggregate reference—and preserve unknown when occlusion or compositing makes the spatial relation unclear. The repeated high-confidence traces are dependent, not independent corroboration; this is a semantic binding/calibration issue, not a transport or schema failure.
